claims.text: Flash heating at approximately 10^5 K/s, with a dwell of about 55 ms and rapid cooling, yields kinetically trapped single-phase solid-solution noble-metal HEA nanoparticles.
The baseline nanoparticles contain more than five elements.
Extending the high-temperature dwell time increases atomic mobility and diffusion.
Increased atomic mobility allows atoms to overcome local kinetic barriers.
Rapid heating followed by immediate quenching kinetically traps the multielement mixture as a metastable, disordered, single-phase solid solution.
Longer high-temperature exposure permits elemental rearrangement that can produce segregation or ordering.
Strong mutual elemental affinities or large differences in mixing enthalpy favor phase separation or thermodynamically more stable ordered structures once diffusion is sufficient.
Extending the dwell beyond the approximately 55 ms baseline will cause phase separation or the emergence of ordered structures rather than preserving the intended disordered single phase.
Nanoparticles subjected to extended dwell times will exhibit additional diffraction peaks or domains relative to the baseline.
The additional peaks or domains will indicate phase separation or ordering.
The hypothesis applies under inert or reductive atmospheres at a baseline peak temperature of about 2000 K.
The proposed intervention is to increase dwell time to values such as 100 ms and 200 ms while holding composition, heating rate, atmosphere, peak temperature, and precursor loading constant.
The hypothesis is limited to chemistries in which diffusion kinetics become dominant in phase selection during extended high-temperature exposure.
The critical dwell time for phase evolution depends on the elemental mixture and synthesis apparatus.
Persistence of the same homogeneous, single-phase disordered structure at the tested extended dwell times, with no detectable segregation or ordering, would falsify the proposed dwell-time mechanism.
